title: Reciprocal Mittag–Leffler functions: complete monotonicity below the parameter band, and the exact boundary near order two
shortTitle: The band is too narrow: when the reciprocal Mittag–Leffler function is completely monotone
oneLine: The reciprocal of the Mittag–Leffler function E is completely monotone for every 0 < β ≤ α when 1 < α < 2, and, for α near 2, exactly for 0 < β ≤ b(α) with b(2) = 3, so the conjectured band α − 1 ≤ β ≤ α is too narrow on both sides.
abstract: For which parameters is the reciprocal 1/E of the two-parameter Mittag–Leffler function completely monotone, and so (after normalising) the Laplace transform of a probability law? Garrappa, Gerhold, Popolizio and Simon (2025, Conjecture 25) proposed that, for 1 < α < 2, this happens exactly when α − 1 ≤ β ≤ α. This candidate proves two results showing the band is too narrow. Theorem A: for every 1 < α < 2 and 0 < β ≤ α, log[Γ(β)E] is a Bernstein function, so every positive power of the normalised reciprocal is the Laplace transform of an infinitely divisible law; this covers the whole triangle below the band. The proof combines a dilation-ratio identity contained in the proof of the authors' Proposition 3 with a classical recurrence that lowers β by one. Theorem B: for α in some neighbourhood of 2, the admissible set is exactly the interval (0, b(α)], where b is real analytic, b(2) = 3 and b′(2) = 1 + 2π Si(2π)/(2I(2π)) ≈ 2.8277, with I(a) the integral of (1 − cos u)/u over (0, a); the boundary is where two negative zeros near −4π² collide, and the associated laws are self-decomposable. Since b(α) > α just below 2, the band fails above as well. A numerical continuation of the boundary curve supports a replacement conjecture, and an exact rational certificate exhibits a failure of the global modulus inequality where Theorem A holds. The neighbourhood in Theorem B is not quantified. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Theorem A (proof): for every 1 < α < 2 and 0 < β ≤ α, log[Γ(β)E] is a Bernstein function, so 1/E is completely monotone and every positive power of the normalised reciprocal is an infinitely divisible probability Laplace transform; this covers the triangle 0 < β < α − 1 below the conjectured band.
Theorem B (proof): for α in a neighbourhood of 2 the admissible set is exactly (0, b(α)], with b real analytic, b(2) = 3, and self-decomposable laws throughout; the band fails above as well as below.
Boundary slope (proof and 90-digit check): b′(2) = 1 + 2π Si(2π)/(2I(2π)) = 2.82768173110428…, where the two negative zeros near −4π² collide.
Separation of properties (proof and exact certificate): below the band, complete monotonicity holds while the global inequality |E(z)| ≥ E(Re z) fails, certified at (α, β, z) = (3/2, 1/4, −60 + i).
Numerics and conjecture (evidence only): the double-zero curve continues smoothly over 1.5 ≤ α ≤ 2.5 with b(α) > α below 2, suggesting C_α = (0, b(α)] for all 1 < α < 2.

narration: The band is too narrow. An Evidence Press briefing. The Mittag-Leffler function is a generalisation of the exponential function, with two parameters, called alpha and beta. It turns up wherever processes relax or wait in unusual ways: in fractional differential equations, in models of materials with memory, and in random processes that look the same at every scale. A useful question is when one over this function is completely monotone, meaning its derivatives alternate in sign. When that happens, the function is the Laplace transform of a probability distribution, which makes it far easier to use and to interpret. In 2025 Garrappa, Gerhold, Popolizio and Simon proved this holds when beta lies in a band from alpha minus one up to alpha, for alpha between one and two, and they conjectured that the band is exactly the right answer. This paper shows the band is too narrow, on both sides. The first result covers every alpha between one and two. Below the band, all the way down to zero, the reciprocal is still completely monotone; in fact its logarithm is a Bernstein function, so every power of it is a probability transform. The proof is short: it combines an identity hidden inside the earlier paper's own argument with a classical recurrence. The second result looks closely at alpha near two. There the exact set of good values of beta is an interval from zero up to a boundary b of alpha. At alpha equal to two the boundary is three, and its slope there is about two point eight three, given by an exact formula. The boundary is where two zeros of the function on the negative axis collide and leave the real line. Because the boundary sits above alpha, the band fails from above as well. What is not proved: how close to two alpha must be, and the full answer for other alpha, which is left as a conjecture supported by computation. This is an anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate, not peer reviewed or independently reproduced. Published on the fourth of November twenty twenty-six, its paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.
